metadata.title: Agreement Is Not Accuracy
metadata.audience: Students and practitioners learning to use and report on AI systems
metadata.fellow: Janvi Chitroda, AI Data Engineer volunteer, Medhavy project, Humanitarians AI
metadata.note: STEM/learning film. Thesis: an ensemble of AI judges measures how often they agree, not whether they're right: a strong routing tool, a weak proof of correctness. Narration supplied verbatim and pre-approved by Janvi (2026-10-27). WORDING LAW: verified/accurate/reliable never describe the definitions; they appear only negated or as words to avoid.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — Claude composer, ask lands answered. Required intro line + AI-narration disclosure + teammate credit.
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Janvi and this video is about why agreement between AI judges is not the same as accuracy. This narration is an AI-generated voice; the work is mine. My teammate Thejus built the definition generation for the Medhavy textbook, and I built the QA pipeline that reviews it.

props.command: Three AI judges all approved this definition. Does that mean it's right?
output: It means the three judges agreed
Not that the definition is right
That needs an expert answer key

show.event: Greeting 'Hi, Janvi' with spark; composer empty
The ask types into the composer
Three answer lines land: agreed / not that it's right / needs an answer key

beats.role_note: The misconception: three judges agree, so it must be right. Three judge cards all show 'approved'; caption 'agreed ≠ right'.
beats.narration_text: Here's the trap. Three AI models read the same definition, and all three say it's fine. That feels like proof. But all you've learned is that they agreed. Whether they're right is a separate question.
beats.visual_intent: One definition at top; three judge cards (Mistral / OpenAI / Claude logos) each stamp 'approved' in turn; a tick-row 'proof?' appears, then the caption 'agreed ≠ right' lands with 'right' in an empty dashed answer slot.

beats.role_note: Reuses Video 1 B04_ThreeJudges: three providers (logos), five tags, 2-of-3 wins, all differ → flagged for a human.
beats.narration_text: The method: use judges from different providers, so their mistakes are less likely to line up. Mine were Mistral Small, G P T four o mini and Claude three point five Sonnet. Each picks one of five tags. Two of three agree, that tag wins. All three differ, it's flagged for a human.
beats.visual_intent: Video 1's three-judges scene: definition label, three judge columns with logos, five tag chips, case 1 approved/approved/supplementary → approved wins, case 2 all differ → flagged for human REVIEW.

show.event: Three judge columns appear on each model's name
All 3 differ → flagged for human REVIEW

beats.role_note: Calibration chart: average scores ~65 / ~76 / ~56; a 70 cutoff would punish the strictest judge; tags are categorical.
beats.narration_text: Vote on tags, not averaged scores. My judges scored on different scales, averaging about 65, 76 and 56. A cutoff of 70 would punish the strictest judge. A tag means the same thing from every judge.
beats.visual_intent: Three vertical bars with logos under them: Mistral Small ~65, GPT-4o-mini ~76, Claude 3.5 Sonnet ~56; a dashed line at 70; Claude's bar marked below the line; then 'approved = approved' tag chip under all three.

show.event: Dashed cutoff at 70; strictest judge falls below
One 'approved' tag means the same from every judge

beats.role_note: Triage at scale: one bar of 10,049 rows splits 94.2% resolved by majority / 5.8% flagged for human review.
beats.narration_text: What it's good for is triage at scale. Across 10,049 rows, 94.2 percent were resolved by majority, and 5.8 percent were flagged for human review.
beats.visual_intent: A single wide bar labelled '10,049 rows' splits into a teal 94.2% segment 'resolved by majority' and a slate 5.8% segment 'flagged for human review'.

beats.role_note: Reuses Video 1 B07_Limitations: no gold standard · shared blind spots · self-preference risk. The required 'when NOT to use it' beat.
beats.narration_text: And when not to trust it. There's no gold standard, so agreement alone says nothing about accuracy. If all three judges share a blind spot, the vote can't see it. And G P T four o mini helped generate some definitions and also judged them, which risks self-preference.
beats.visual_intent: Video 1's three limitation panels: no gold standard (vote vs empty answer key), shared blind spots (three overlapping circles), self-preference risk (OpenAI writes → judges).

beats.role_note: Vocabulary: SAY inter-model agreement, consensus / AVOID verified, accurate, reliable (struck, Video 1 strike style).
beats.narration_text: So report what you measured: inter-model agreement, or consensus. Not verified, accurate or reliable, unless you checked against expert answers.
beats.visual_intent: Two columns. SAY (teal): 'inter-model agreement', 'consensus', highlighted in amber. AVOID (burnt orange): 'verified', 'accurate', 'reliable', each struck on the spoken word. Footer: 'unless checked against expert answers'.

show.event: AVOID column: verified, accurate, reliable struck
Footer: unless checked against expert answers

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — suggested prompt typed, read aloud, then discussed.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Before you claim accuracy, have an expert label a small sample. Compare the ensemble's tags to those labels. That match rate, not agreement, tells you how often the vote is right.

props.command: Before I claim accuracy: have an expert label a small sample, compare my ensemble's tags to those labels, and report the match rate.

show.event: 'Your turn.' greeting; the suggested prompt types into the composer as it is read
